title: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle, and find the node where the cycle begins, using Floyd's two-pointer algorithm in constant space.
shortTitle: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
topicTitle: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle

s1_definition.profdef: Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm, the tortoise and hare, uses two pointers that advance through a linked list at different speeds, one node at a time and two nodes at a time. If there is no cycle the fast pointer reaches the end; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps and meets the slow pointer inside the loop. A short second phase then locates the cycle's start. It runs in linear time using only two pointers, so constant extra space.

A supervisor sends two auditors down the chain, a slow one stepping one record at a time and a fast one stepping two at a time. If the chain simply ends, the fast auditor falls off the end and there is no loop. But if the chain secretly loops, the fast auditor keeps circling and inevitably catches up to the slow one from behind, and their meeting proves a loop exists without the supervisor ever needing to write down which records were already visited.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm, the tortoise and hare, uses two pointers that advance through a linked list at different speeds, one node at a time and two nodes at a time. If there is no cycle the fast pointer reaches the end; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps and meets the slow pointer inside the loop. A short second phase then locates the cycle's start. It runs in linear time using only two pointers, so constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India chains transaction records together, each pointing to the next, and a corrupted chain might accidentally loop back on itself, which would make any traversal run forever. A supervisor sends two auditors down the chain, a slow one stepping one record at a time and a fast one stepping two at a time. If the chain simply ends, the fast auditor falls off the end and there is no loop. But if the chain secretly loops, the fast auditor keeps circling and inevitably catches up to the slow one from behind, and their meeting proves a loop exists without the supervisor ever needing to write down which records were already visited.

**One line to remember:** Advance a slow pointer by one and a fast pointer by two; if they meet there is a cycle, and a reset-and-walk phase finds its start.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive way to detect a cycle is to record every visited node in a hash set and flag a repeat, which works but uses linear extra space. Floyd's algorithm achieves the same in constant space, which is its whole appeal, by exploiting the fact that two pointers moving at different speeds in a loop must eventually collide.

In the detection phase you move slow by one node and fast by two nodes each step. You guard the fast pointer carefully: the loop continues while fast and fast's next are both non-null, because fast reads two links ahead. If fast reaches null, the list ended, so there is no cycle. If slow and fast ever reference the same node, they met inside a loop, proving a cycle exists. The reason they must meet is that once both are inside the loop, the fast pointer gains one step on the slow pointer every move, so the gap shrinks by one each step until it is zero, guaranteeing a collision.

Finding the cycle's entry point is a beautiful second phase that falls out of the math. After the meeting, you reset one pointer to the head and leave the other at the meeting node, then advance both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the cycle's start. This works because the distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start when measured around the loop, a consequence of the speed ratio. It is a result worth being able to justify rather than just memorise.

A senior-level nuance is where this matters and its alternatives. Cycle detection prevents infinite traversal in corrupted linked structures, and the same tortoise-and-hare idea detects cycles in functional iteration such as finding a repeated value in a sequence defined by a function, and underlies the "find the duplicate number" problem by treating array indices as links. The hash-set approach is simpler to write and sometimes preferred for clarity when memory is not a concern, so I state the space-time trade-off explicitly and choose Floyd's when constant space is required.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India links transaction records in a chain for sequential processing, and a data-corruption bug can make a record point back into the chain, creating a loop that would make the processor traverse forever. We must detect such a loop safely and in constant space because the chains can be very long. This is exactly Floyd's cycle detection.

Problem 2 — Beyond knowing a loop exists, the repair tool must identify the exact record where the loop re-enters, so it can be cut. The second phase of Floyd's algorithm locates that entry node precisely.

In our mini-project we build a `ChainCycleDetector` over a simple linked node of transaction IDs. The demo builds one clean chain and one chain with an injected loop, detects the cycle, and reports the entry node ID.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a clean chain T1 to T2 to T3 to T4 to null, then the same chain with T4's next pointed back to T2 to create a loop.

Step 1: For the clean chain, slow and fast both start at T1. Slow moves to T2 and fast moves to T3. Slow moves to T3 and fast moves to null, because T4's next is null.

Step 2: The loop condition checks fast, which is now null, so the loop ends. Since the pointers never met and fast reached the end, there is no cycle, and we return null. The demo reports no cycle for the clean chain.

Step 3: For the corrupted chain, T4 now points back to T2, so T2, T3, T4 form a loop. Slow and fast start at T1. Slow goes to T2, fast goes to T3.

Step 4: Slow goes to T3, fast goes two steps from T3 to T4 to T2, landing on T2. Slow goes to T4, fast goes from T2 to T3 to T4, landing on T4. Now slow and fast both reference T4, so they met, proving a cycle exists.

Step 5: Begin phase two to find the entry. Reset a fresh pointer to the head T1 and keep the met pointer at T4. Advance both one step: the head pointer goes T1 to T2, and the met pointer goes T4 to T2.

Step 6: Both pointers now reference T2, so they meet at T2, which is exactly where the loop re-enters the chain. We return T2, and the demo reports the cycle entry as T2, all achieved with just two pointers and no visited set.

```
[2026-10-26 23:43:01] INFO    Clean chain cycle entry: none
[2026-10-26 23:43:01] INFO    Corrupted chain cycle entry: T2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  clean:  T1 → T2 → T3 → T4 → null
    slow/fast advance 1/2 → fast hits null → no cycle

  corrupted:  T1 → T2 → T3 → T4 ┐
                     ▲──────────┘   (T4.next = T2)

  Phase1 detect:  slow +1, fast +2 → meet at T4 (inside loop)
  Phase2 entry:   p=head(T1), slow=meet(T4); step both by 1
                  T1→T2 , T4→T2  → meet at T2 = cycle start
```

```
  │  ───────────────────────  │───────▶│  id: String        │
  │  + cycleStart(head):TxnNode│       │  next: TxnNode     │
  └───────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────┘
      Post: entry node if cycle else null; O(n) time, O(1) space

  ── State Diagram: Pointers ──────────────────────────────

  [fast reaches null] ──→ no cycle (return null)
  [slow == fast]      ──→ cycle found → phase 2
  [phase 2: p==slow]  ──→ return entry node

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. cycleStart: slow+=1, fast+=2 until null or meet
  2.   meet → reset p=head; step p & slow by 1 until equal
  3.   return p (entry) or null
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm, the tortoise and hare, uses two pointers moving through a linked list at different speeds, slow by one node and fast by two nodes each step. If there is no cycle, the fast pointer runs off the end of the list. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer keeps circling and inevitably catches the slow pointer from behind, and their meeting proves a cycle exists. The whole appeal over the obvious hash-set approach is that this uses only two pointers, so constant extra space, in linear time.

In the detection phase I guard the fast pointer carefully, continuing only while fast and fast's next are both non-null because fast reads two links ahead, and if fast reaches null I return no cycle. The reason the pointers must meet inside a loop is that once both are in it, the fast pointer gains exactly one step on the slow pointer every move, so the gap shrinks by one each step until it hits zero. To find where the cycle begins, there is an elegant second phase: I reset one pointer to the head, leave the other at the meeting node, and advance both one step at a time, and they meet exactly at the cycle's start, because the distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry around the loop.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on chains of linked transaction records, where a data-corruption bug could make a record point back into the chain and cause the processor to traverse forever. Floyd's algorithm detected such a loop safely in constant space even on very long chains, and the second phase pinpointed the exact record where the loop re-entered so the repair tool could cut it.

The senior-level point I make is the space-time trade-off and the reach of the idea. The hash-set method is simpler to write and fine when memory is not a concern, so I state that explicitly and choose Floyd's when constant space is required. I also note that the same tortoise-and-hare principle detects cycles in any sequence defined by repeatedly applying a function, which is how the classic find-the-duplicate-number problem is solved by treating array values as links, so recognising this pattern unlocks a family of constant-space cycle problems.
